items.text: Hey, come on in. Good to see you again. Have a seat wherever's comfortable.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Thanks. It's been a rough couple of weeks, honestly.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: I appreciate you saying that up front. Let's get into it. What's been going on?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'm here for my med follow-up. The sertraline isn't doing what it was doing for me a few months ago. And my sleep has gotten really bad.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Okay. So we're looking at depression breakthrough and worsening insomnia. Anything else on your mind today?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Some anxiety stuff too. Panic-y feelings off and on. But the depression and sleep are the biggest things.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Tell me about the depression. When did you start noticing it slipping?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Probably six weeks ago. It was creeping up before then but I told myself it was just a busy patch at school.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Mood?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Low. Most days I'm flat. I'd say a four out of ten if ten is normal for me.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Anhedonia?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yeah. I haven't picked up my guitar in a month. Used to play almost every day.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Energy?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Tanked. I'm exhausted by mid-afternoon even when I sleep okay, which I'm not.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Concentration, focus?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Bad. I'm rereading the same paragraph four times. I missed a deadline last week, which I never do.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Appetite?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Down. I've lost about five pounds in the last month.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Some passive thoughts. Like, wishing I wasn't here. But no plan. No intent.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Thank you for telling me. We'll come back to safety. Any thoughts of harming anyone else?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No. Never.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Self-harm? Cutting, anything like that?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, none of that.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Let's talk about the sleep. What does a typical night look like?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I fall asleep okay around eleven. But I wake up at two or three and just lie there. I'll eventually get an hour back around five but it's not real sleep.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: So middle insomnia mostly, not initial?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Right.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any caffeine in the afternoon, alcohol close to bed?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I cut caffeine after noon already. I'll have a glass of wine maybe twice a week, never right before bed.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Are you using anything to help you sleep?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Just OTC melatonin, five milligrams. Doesn't really do anything.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: And the anxiety. Tell me more.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Constant rumination. My brain just won't quit. And about once a week I'll have a stretch of, like, racing heart, can't breathe, hands shaking. Lasts maybe ten minutes.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Panic episodes.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yeah.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Triggers, or out of nowhere?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Mix. Sometimes school stress kicks one off. Sometimes I'll just be standing in line at the grocery store.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Quick screening — any new physical symptoms, headaches, chest pain, GI issues?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No.
items.speaker: UNSPECIFIED

items.text: Any changes in your thyroid energy, hair, temperature?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, that's been stable.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: No fevers, no infections lately?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Let me make sure I have your psych history straight. You were first diagnosed with depression at twenty-two.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Right. Junior year of college.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: And we've previously tried fluoxetine — didn't work — and bupropion — caused agitation.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yeah, the bupropion made me feel like I was vibrating.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: No psychiatric hospitalizations, no ECT.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, never been admitted.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any past suicide attempts?
items.speaker: UNSPECIFIED

items.text: No.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Past medical history — hypothyroidism.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Diagnosed five years ago, on levothyroxine ever since.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Anything else?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, that's it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Family psychiatric history.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Mom has bipolar, type two. Dad's an alcoholic, in recovery now. My older sister has depression.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any suicide in the family?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: An uncle, on my dad's side, when I was a kid.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Sorry to hear that.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Social. You're a grad student still.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Second year. PhD program.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Living with your partner.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yeah, three years now.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Alcohol?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Two or three drinks a week. Wine mostly.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Recreational drugs, cannabis?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, none.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Tobacco, vaping?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Exercise?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I run a couple times a week, or I did. Hasn't happened in two weeks honestly.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Stressors?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Just the usual academic pressure. Nothing acute.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Med list. You're on sertraline one hundred milligrams daily.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Every morning, yeah.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Levothyroxine fifty micrograms daily.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Right, on an empty stomach.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: And you mentioned melatonin five milligrams at bedtime, OTC.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yep.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Anything else? Vitamins, supplements, anything I'm missing?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I take a multivitamin. That's it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any aspirin, ibuprofen regularly?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, only occasionally for cramps.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Drug allergies — your chart says no known drug allergies. Still accurate?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Still no allergies that I know of.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Food, environmental?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Nothing.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Quick vitals from intake. Blood pressure 118 over 74, pulse 82, respirations 16.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Okay.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Temperature 98.4. Weight 132 pounds. Height 5 feet 5 inches.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Down five from last visit.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: I see that. We'll watch it.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'm going to dictate my mental status exam as we go. Patient is alert, oriented to person, place, time, situation.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Mm-hmm.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Appearance well-groomed, dressed appropriately. Eye contact good, slightly downcast. Mood patient describes as low. Affect constricted, congruent with stated mood.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Sounds about right.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Speech normal rate, rhythm, prosody. Thought process linear, goal-directed. No flight of ideas, no thought blocking. Thought content — passive suicidal ideation as discussed, no active intent, no plan, no homicidal ideation, no perceptual disturbances, no delusions.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Good.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Insight and judgment fair. Cognition grossly intact. Memory recent and remote intact for what we discussed.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: PHQ-9 today scored 16 — moderately severe depression. GAD-7 was 12, moderate anxiety.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Higher than last time.
items.speaker: UNSPECIFIED

items.text: Yeah, both up. Last visit you were a 9 and a 7. So we're seeing a real shift.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Labs from two weeks ago — TSH 2.1, well within range. CBC was normal. Comprehensive metabolic panel normal. So this isn't a thyroid contribution.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I figured the thyroid was fine.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: It is.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Alright. Assessment and plan. Problem one — major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate to severe based on today's PHQ-9.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Okay.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Going to increase your sertraline to 150 milligrams daily. Take it the same way you've been taking the 100 — in the morning with food.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: 150. Got it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Side effects to watch for in the first couple weeks — GI upset, headache, increased agitation, any worsening of suicidal thoughts. Any of those, you call me.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I will.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: If we don't see meaningful improvement in four weeks, we'll talk about augmenting with bupropion at a lower dose, or switching class entirely.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Problem two — generalized anxiety disorder, moderate.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Yeah.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: I expect the sertraline bump will help the anxiety too — they often track together. I'd like to defer adding a benzodiazepine for now. We'll reassess in four weeks.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'd rather not be on a benzo if I can avoid it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Same, glad we agree.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Problem three — insomnia, secondary to depression and anxiety.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: The sleep is the worst part.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Starting trazodone 50 milligrams at bedtime. Take it 30 minutes before you want to sleep. May feel a little groggy in the morning at first, that fades within a week.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Trazodone, 50, at bedtime. Got it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: You can stop the melatonin — trazodone will do the work. Sleep hygiene basics — same wake time every day even on weekends, no screens an hour before bed.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'll try.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Problem four — hypothyroidism, well controlled.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Stable.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Continue levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily. We'll recheck TSH in six months.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I also want to refer you back to therapy. Have you been seeing anyone?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Not for about a year. My old therapist moved out of state.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: I'm going to refer you to a CBT-trained therapist. Cognitive behavioral therapy alongside meds is going to give you the best outcomes here, especially with the rumination piece.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'm open to it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: I'll send you a few names.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Safety plan. If those passive thoughts get more active — start showing up with a plan, with intent — what's your step one?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Call you. Or call my partner.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Right. And if it's after hours and you can't reach me, you call 988 or you go to the ER. We can also use the crisis text line — text HOME to 741741. I'll write that down for you.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Okay.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Are there any firearms in the home?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Any large quantities of medications you'd want to put in your partner's care for now?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: I'll have them keep my sertraline. That makes sense.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Few follow-up items. Add a task to call the patient in two weeks for a mood check-in — I want to know how the dose increase is landing.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Two weeks, okay.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Add a task for the MA to schedule the CBT therapist referral within a week — let's not let that drift.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Good.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: And add a task to recheck TSH in six months so we don't lose track of that.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Sounds good.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Follow-up appointment in four weeks for med check. Sooner if anything changes.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: What if the trazodone makes me too groggy?
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Cut to 25 milligrams and call me. We can adjust.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Okay.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Anything else for me before we wrap?
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: No, I think we covered it.
items.speaker: PATIENT

items.text: Take care of yourself. I'll see you in four weeks.
items.speaker: DOCTOR

items.text: Thanks.
items.speaker: PATIENT
